1. The animation shows how inflation erodes a fixed income payment. An illustrative retiree, Ruth, gets a check. The row of crates next to it stands for what that check can buy. The label says US consumer prices (CPI-U).

2. Over time the check shrinks a little in each frame, and the row of crates stays the same length at first. By frame 5, Ruth is at age 85. The check is labeled "check: +2% a year", and the row has nine light crates and one dark, faded crate. Frame 6 adds "about 9 in 10" and "first check: 10 crates". The dark crate is the one that is gone.

3. A check that stays flat buys less as prices rise. The first check bought 10 crates' worth of goods. At age 85, with a check growing 2% a year, it buys about 9 of those 10. So even a payment that rises 2% a year may not fully keep up with US price increases. The frames label this as illustrative, US-only, and "history, not a forecast".

4. The frames give no explicit advice. A viewer in my position, 64 and comparing two payout options, might take this away: when comparing a flat payout with one that rises over time, think about what the check will buy years from now, not just its size today. The frames don't say which option to choose.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion. The animation only shows the effect of inflation on purchasing power and does not tell the viewer what to do. The "history, not a forecast" label also suggests it avoids predicting future inflation or recommending a choice.
